title: Add momentum/trend-following layer to capture signals the bot is already seeing
analysis: The journal reveals a structural contradiction: the bot is repeatedly generating and then discarding momentum signals. On 2026-05-18, AAPL fired 'RSI>65 (strong momentum)', 'AboveMA20>1%', 'ADX>25 (trending)' with a 3.95 R:R and was SUBMITTED — this is a momentum entry, not mean reversion. On 2026-05-20, AMD fired identical momentum signals at 2.0 R:R and was also SUBMITTED. Both trades were placed under a mean reversion system that explicitly bans entries when ADX>30. These trades succeeded in clearing the R:R gate (1.5:1 minimum), yet they are structurally misclassified. Meanwhile, the 4 META BUY attempts on 2026-05-19 (signal score 4, R:R 3.1–3.36, legitimate mean reversion signals: RSI<45, BelowMA20>1%, ADX<25) were all REJECTED solely because of the existing-position rule — the bot had valid mean reversion setups it could not execute. The macro context supports this dual approach: SPY is above its 20-day MA ($742.72 vs $730.00, +1.74%), VIX is 16.76 (low, non-fearful), Technology +1.33% and Healthcare +2.10% over 5 days signal a risk-on, trending tape. This is not a pure ranging environment. The system is leaving money on both sides: blocking mean reversion re-entries (META) and mislabeling momentum trades as mean reversion entries.
rationale: A single-strategy system in a mixed regime (SPY trending above MA20, VIX low, tech leading) will structurally underperform. The bot is already taking momentum trades — it just isn't accounting for them properly, which means risk rules, sizing, and exit logic designed for mean reversion are being misapplied to trend entries. Formalizing a second strategy layer with its own entry logic, exit rules (trail with ATR rather than target the MA20), and regime filter (ADX>25 required, not prohibited) would let the system operate correctly in both ranging and trending sub-regimes without the current identity confusion.

insight.why_now: Two of the three actual trade submissions in the observed window (AAPL 2026-05-18, AMD 2026-05-20) fired explicitly momentum signals (RSI>65, ADX>25) that contradict mean reversion logic. The system is already trading momentum — it just lacks the framework to do it correctly. SPY sitting 1.74% above its 20-day MA in a low-VIX environment means the ranging regime assumption is partially wrong right now.
insight.purpose: Create a formally separated momentum/trend entry path with its own signal scoring, position sizing, and exit rules, so the system stops applying mean reversion exits (target = MA20) to momentum trades that should be trailed with ATR stops.
insight.expected_effect: Captures the trending moves that the current system accidentally enters but mismanages. Reduces the structural drag of applying wrong exit logic to momentum positions. Allows the META-style mean reversion re-entries to proceed on their own track without being blocked by momentum positions held in the same slot.
insight.risks: Adding a second strategy increases system complexity and the risk of signal bleed — a momentum trade being miscategorized as mean reversion or vice versa. Regime detection must be robust. In a whipsaw market, both strategies can lose simultaneously, increasing correlation of drawdowns.

current_rule: 6. TREND FILTER: If ADX > 30, regime is TRENDING — do NOT take mean reversion signals.
proposed_rule: 6. REGIME ROUTING: Classify each signal set before entry. If ADX > 25 AND RSI > 60 AND price > MA20 by >1%, route to MOMENTUM mode: use ATR trailing stop (1.5x ATR), target 3x ATR extension, do NOT use MA20 as take-profit. If ADX < 25 AND RSI < 45 AND price < MA20, route to MEAN REVERSION mode: existing rules apply. If signals conflict across modes, SKIP. Never apply mean reversion exits to momentum entries or vice versa.

title: Symbol fixation on META causing repeated wasted cycles and opportunity cost
analysis: On 2026-05-19, the bot attempted to BUY META four separate times across a 75-minute window (12:39, 12:52, 13:40, 13:55), each time generating a legitimate signal score of 4 with R:R between 3.10 and 3.36 — all meeting entry criteria — and each time being correctly rejected because 16 shares of META were already held. This is not a risk management success; it is a signal generation failure. The bot consumed 4 of approximately 8 decision cycles on that day re-evaluating the same blocked symbol instead of scanning for alternative setups. On the same day, 8 SKIP entries with signal_score=0 followed, suggesting no alternative was found. The pattern indicates the watchlist or scanning logic has insufficient breadth to surface substitute opportunities when a top-ranked symbol is unavailable. The META entries had valid mean reversion setups (RSI<45, BelowMA20>1%, ADX<25, PositiveSentiment) — these signals were real. The failure is that no comparable setup on a different symbol was identified to absorb that signal energy. Account was down ~$100–$160 for the day with 3 open positions and no new entries made despite valid market conditions.
rationale: Repeated re-evaluation of a blocked symbol is a behavioral inefficiency that wastes decision cycles and creates implicit anchoring to a specific ticker. The system should detect when a symbol has been rejected due to existing position within the same session and suppress it from re-evaluation for the remainder of that session, then redirect scanning effort to substitute symbols with similar factor profiles.

insight.why_now: Four consecutive META rejections in 75 minutes on 2026-05-19 is the clearest pattern in the dataset. This is not occasional — it is systematic scanner behavior that needs a circuit breaker.
insight.purpose: Eliminate wasted decision cycles on blocked symbols, force diversification of scan attention, and reduce the implicit single-stock anchoring that prevents the system from finding substitute mean reversion setups.
insight.expected_effect: On days like 2026-05-19 where valid mean reversion conditions existed but the primary candidate was blocked, the system would redirect to 2-3 alternative symbols with similar profiles (e.g., other large-cap tech in ADX<25 ranging mode), potentially converting wasted SKIP cycles into actual entries.
insight.risks: Forcing substitute entries when the primary signal is blocked may result in lower-quality setups being taken. The substitute symbol must still independently meet all signal thresholds — this rule must not lower the bar, only redirect attention.

proposed_rule: SYMBOL SUPPRESSION RULE: If a BUY signal is generated for a symbol but rejected due to an existing open position in that symbol, suppress that symbol from re-evaluation for the remainder of the trading session. Flag the rejection in the scan log and immediately re-run the full watchlist scan to identify the next-best qualifying symbol. Do not re-evaluate the same blocked symbol more than once per session.

title: Low-VIX regime warrants commission-aware sizing and tighter opportunity filter
analysis: VIX is at 16.76 — firmly in the low-volatility zone (below 20). SPY is $742.72 vs MA20 of $730.00, sitting 1.74% above its 20-day average. Sector data shows Healthcare +2.10% and Technology +1.33% as 5-day leaders, with Energy -0.52% and Industrials -0.51% lagging — a mild risk-on rotation, not defensive positioning. In low-VIX environments, mean reversion still works but the oscillations are smaller, meaning take-profit targets compress while commissions and spread costs remain fixed. The current stop loss is set at 0.5x ATR — in a low-volatility regime, ATR itself is smaller, so both the stop and the profit target shrink in absolute dollar terms. The R:R gate of 1.5:1 minimum is still being met (META entries showed 3.1–3.36 R:R), but the gross dollar P&L per trade compresses. The journal shows the account has drifted from ~$98,500 to ~$98,677 over the observed window — roughly flat with high cycle activity. The system is not losing, but the low-vol environment means it is grinding for small gains while running full position sizing (1.5% risk per trade). At 1.5% risk on a ~$98,500 account, each trade risks ~$1,477. In a low-VIX tape with tight ATR, this may represent oversizing relative to the actual move potential.
rationale: VIX below 15-17 compresses realized volatility, which shrinks ATR-based stops and targets proportionally. Running the same 1.5% risk-per-trade in a low-vol regime as in a normal regime creates asymmetry: the percentage of account risked stays constant but the dollar profit opportunity per trade shrinks. Introducing a VIX-scaled position sizing modifier preserves the R:R structure while right-sizing exposure to the actual opportunity available in the current tape.

insight.why_now: VIX at 16.76 with SPY above MA20 is the current macro state. The account has been essentially flat ($98,284 to $98,677 over the journal window) despite valid signals firing and positions being held. This suggests the low-vol environment is compressing returns while risk per trade remains at full sizing.
insight.purpose: Scale position size dynamically with volatility regime so that in low-VIX environments the system takes appropriately sized bets relative to the compressed move potential, and in higher-VIX environments (20-25) does not automatically over-size into wider but more dangerous swings.
insight.expected_effect: In the current low-VIX (16.76) environment, a modest sizing reduction of 15-20% (e.g., 1.5% → 1.25% risk per trade) reduces commission drag as a percentage of gross P&L while keeping the strategy active. In VIX > 22 environments, the rule would also prevent oversizing into dangerous vol expansions. Net effect: smoother equity curve with less dead weight from commissions in quiet markets.
insight.risks: Dynamic sizing adds a parameter that must be calibrated. If VIX spikes rapidly (flash events), the system may be caught with undersized positions in a regime that briefly offers large mean reversion opportunities. A hard floor on sizing (never below 0.75% risk per trade) should be maintained.

current_rule: 1. POSITION SIZE: Risk per trade = 1.5% of account (medium_safety). Max position = 10% of account.
proposed_rule: 1. POSITION SIZE: Risk per trade is VIX-scaled. Base risk = 1.5% of account. If VIX < 17: use 1.0% risk (low-vol regime, compressed moves). If VIX 17–24: use 1.5% risk (normal regime, base sizing). If VIX 25–32: use 1.0% risk (elevated fear, widen stops, reduce size). If VIX > 32: use 0.5% risk or SKIP entirely. Max position = 10% of account at all VIX levels. Floor: never risk less than 0.5% per trade.
